body: This place is a small but very meaningful sea turtle rescue and conservation center, and visiting it was a truly special experience. The center focuses on protecting and rehabilitating sea turtles, and during the visit you can see around ten large turtles that are currently being cared for. In addition, there is a separate area dedicated to turtle eggs, which are protected until they are ready to hatch. It is very interesting to learn about the different stages of the turtles’ lives and the challenges they face in the wild.The entrance fee is 2,000 Sri Lankan rupees per person, and it includes a personal guided tour. Although the visit itself is quite short, lasting about half an hour, it feels well organized and informative. The guide was extremely kind, friendly, and knowledgeable. He patiently answered all of our questions and explained the importance of sea turtle conservation in a clear and engaging way. You can really feel that the staff care deeply about the turtles and their mission.The place itself is not very large, but that does not take away from the experience. On the contrary, the small size makes the visit feel more personal and focused. Most importantly, all of the income from visitors goes directly toward rescuing and protecting the turtles, which makes the visit feel worthwhile and responsible.Overall, this is a great stop for anyone who cares about wildlife, conservation, and ethical tourism. Even though it is a short visit, it is educational, touching, and definitely worth supporting.

body: If you're expecting a genuine turtle rescue experience driven by empathy and conservation, prepare to be bitterly disappointed. This place may claim to be a sanctuary for injured turtles, but its pricing model reveals a far more cynical agenda: exploiting tourists under the guise of charity.Let’s be clear—charging 2000 LKR for foreigners and 1000 LKR for locals for the exact same barebones walkthrough is not just unfair, it’s ethically bankrupt. If this facility truly exists to rescue and rehabilitate turtles, why is there a need to discriminate based on ethnicity? The justification that fees go toward "upkeep and rescue efforts" collapses under scrutiny when the facility itself is shockingly basic, with minimal infrastructure and low overheads. Where exactly is that extra 1000 LKR going?This isn’t a national park or a government-run heritage site—this is a private setup leveraging the emotional pull of sick animals to fleece empathetic visitors. It’s one thing for commercial attractions to charge more for tourists (as distasteful as that is), but to do so in the name of injured wildlife is downright sickening.The turtles deserve better. And so do the people who come hoping to support a good cause. Until this place aligns its pricing with its supposed values, it remains a sham cloaked in sympathy.
title: A Disgraceful Exploitation Disguised as Compassion

body: Mahamodara Sea Turtle Hatchery, Galle Just wanted to post a recommendation for this family-run Sea Turtle Hatchery. My friend and I visited here in August 2025. We were staying in Galle and simply took a short tuk tuk ride to get there. It is not a large place and was inexpensive to go in. We were given a short tour by one of the family and were then able to stay for as long as we wanted.There were some of all of the different Sri Lankan sea turtles at the centre, at various ages and in various stages of recovery. The centre rescues sick and injured turtles, nurses them back to health and releases them back into the wild. They also collect eggs from the beaches and buy them from fishermen before re-burying them safely at the hatchery, releasing them back into the sea after they have hatched. You can pay an additional fee per turtle to release the babies into the sea yourself - which we did. The centre is on the edge of the beach and the family took us there when the conditions for release were favourable. It was a very magical experience for us.Watching the turtles was fascinating and we discovered that they really enjoy having their shells gently scratched, some of them even holding on to the side of the tank to make it easier! We also really enjoyed watching the hermit crabs scuttling about in the sand in their shells - they are really fast! We spent a couple of hours there, talking to the family, savouring a mango lassi from the cafe there and marvelling at the turtles. It was a great and memorable experience.

body: We visited this place and ended up volunteering here. Caring for the turtles is a fulltime job (day and night work) that is why an entrance fee is needed. You should come here because you care about turtles and not because you think you or your children can just come and play with turtles. There have been incidents where people/children dropped a turtle and it died afterwards. So bear this in mind when coming here.The health of the turtles comes in first, and that is how it should be. The rescued sick and injured turtles are brought in to recover and will be put back in the sea once they are healthy again.P.s. if you are interested in volunteering just go there and have a chat with them.
